headline: USDA rewrites hemp crop insurance to match new THC limits for 2027
dek: USDA told insurers on 18 November that hemp policies will follow the new THC definition from the 2027 crop year, leaving hot crops uncovered.
key_points: USDA's Risk Management Agency issued bulletin PM-26-070 on 18 November, updating the federal Hemp Crop Provisions to match the hemp law Congress passed in November 2025.
The new rules take effect with the 30 November 2026 contract change date and apply from the 2027 crop year; insurers must tell growers at least 30 days before their cancellation dates.
Losses caused by THC above the legal limit stay uninsured, but a grower whose crop was also hit by a covered event such as weather may still be paid for that part of the loss.
Growers must tell their insurer within 72 hours of getting THC results, a new paperwork clock that lands as the total-THC rule takes effect on 11 December.
body: The federal crop insurance programme for hemp is being rewritten to follow the stricter THC rules that take effect next month. In a product management bulletin dated 18 November, USDA's Risk Management Agency (RMA) told approved insurance providers that the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation is updating the Hemp Crop Provisions so that allowable THC levels comply with the continuing appropriations act Congress passed in November 2025, the law that redefined hemp.

The change takes effect with the 30 November 2026 contract change date and applies to the 2027 and later crop years, according to the bulletin, signed by RMA Deputy Administrator Richard H. Flournoy. The revised provisions, numbered 27-1218, are due on the RMA website by 30 November. Insurers must notify growers of the changes at least 30 days before each policy's cancellation date.
## What the bulletin changes

The hemp update is one of three items in bulletin PM-26-070; the others correct rice margin price provisions and a malting barley formula. For hemp, the core change is how the policy decides what counts as hemp at all. According to The Marijuana Herald's reading of the new provisions, policies will now point to the definition of hemp in the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, as amended, together with federal regulations and any state or tribal requirements, rather than carrying their own fixed THC figure.

That matters because the federal definition itself is changing. From 11 December, hemp is measured on total THC, which counts THCA, the acid form that turns into THC when heated, and not only delta-9 THC. Plants that tested as compliant under the old delta-9 method can fail under a total-THC test. The same law sets a separate cap of 0.4 milligrams of THC and similar cannabinoids per container for finished hemp products; the Herald notes that the insurance provisions do not apply that consumer-product cap to harvested crops.
> Insurance is where the new THC math stops being a policy argument and becomes a loss a farmer has to carry alone.
## Hot crops stay uninsured

The revised provisions make plain that losses caused by THC above the applicable limit are not covered, whether the limit is federal, set by the state or tribe where the crop is grown, or written into the policy, the Herald reported. A crop that must be destroyed because it tested hot is the grower's loss, not the insurer's.

The rules do carve out a middle case. When an insured crop is damaged by a covered cause, such as bad weather, and then fails THC testing, insurers must still account for the affected production through inspections and appraisals. A payment may be available for the part of the loss the covered cause produced, while the THC-related part stays excluded, according to the Herald.
## New deadlines for growers

The definitions themselves are simpler. The revised provisions define hemp by reference to 7 U.S.C. 1639o, the hemp section of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, and trim the policy's own definitions of CBD and THC, according to the summary of changes in the provisions. Because the policy now points to the statute rather than restating a limit, a future change by Congress to the hemp definition should flow into coverage without a separate rewrite. That reading is ours.

The provisions add procedural duties. Growers must notify their insurer within 72 hours of receiving THC test results from the governing authority, the Herald reported. If a damaged field needs to be harvested before final THC results are in, the grower must first get the insurer's consent. The provisions keep a separate 72-hour rule for licences: if the state, tribal or federal licence that lets a grower produce hemp is terminated or suspended during the crop year, the grower must tell the insurer within 72 hours, and all of that crop's acreage becomes uninsured with no premium or indemnity due. Missing any of these steps could complicate a claim, so growers who buy federal coverage will need to align testing schedules, harvest plans and paperwork more tightly than before.

The dedicated hemp policy covers production grown for CBD, fiber, grain and other approved uses. The Herald said the changes are separate from revisions USDA made earlier this year to its Whole-Farm Revenue Protection programme, which some diversified growers use instead.
## Why it lands now

The bulletin arrives in the middle of a crowded month for hemp. The federal product limits take effect on 11 December unless Congress acts; as we reported on 18 November, Senators Tim Sheehy and Amy Klobuchar have filed a bill to replace that ban with federal regulation. Separately, as we reported on 17 November, USDA's enforcement discretion that lets hemp be tested at labs without DEA registration runs out on 31 December, putting a second compliance change on growers in the same window.

The crop insurance change does not depend on the outcome of the fight over finished products. Even if Congress delays the 0.4 milligram container cap, the move to total THC for plants is what drives the insurance rule, and the bulletin ties coverage to whatever definition is in force. In practice, a grower planting high-CBD varieties in 2027 faces a higher chance of a hot test under total THC and no insurance backstop for that outcome.
## What it means

For flower and CBD growers, the safest reading is that genetics and harvest timing now carry more financial risk, because the insurance product will not absorb a failed test. For fiber and grain growers, whose varieties sit far below the limits, the change is mostly paperwork: the 72-hour notice and the consent rule. For lenders that require crop insurance as a condition of operating loans, the clearer exclusion may push them to ask harder questions about varieties and testing plans before they lend. That last point is our assessment, not a statement from USDA.
## What to watch

Watch for the final Hemp Crop Provisions (27-1218) on the RMA website by 30 November, and for insurers' notices to growers ahead of 2027 cancellation dates. On 11 December the total-THC definition and the product cap take effect unless Congress changes them in a funding bill or passes the Sheehy-Klobuchar proposal. On 1 January 2027 the DEA-registered lab requirement for hemp testing takes effect unless USDA extends its enforcement discretion again.
